idiom_name: Jetpack Navigation: NavController as the single coordinator over a navigation graph
implementation_notes: On Android the platform library is the Application Controller: the navigation graph (an XML resource or the Kotlin DSL) declares every destination and the actions between them, NavController is the single coordinator that swaps destinations inside a NavHost, owns the back stack, resolves deep links and applies safe-args, and callers only issue navigate(R.id.amount) or popBackStack(). That graph plus controller replaces the classic controller-plus-command objects: destinations are the steps, actions are the transitions, and per-conversation state rides in view models scoped to a graph entry (or to the graph itself) instead of in the Activity. Use it for screen-shaped flows; for message-shaped or server-side flows, model the workflow explicitly (a sealed-class state machine service, or Spring Web Flow on the JVM) - and keep the decision in one class rather than scattering navigate() calls through composables.
pitfalls: The graph is compiled and checked, but destinations reachable only through nested graphs are easy to orphan; the graph is code and needs review and tests (TestNavHostController) like code.

navigate() must be called on the main thread from a live destination: calling it from a background coroutine or after the fragment is detached throws, so events belong to the current destination's lifecycle.
Duplicating navigation decisions inside composables or deep-link handlers makes the graph and the code disagree; deep links must resolve through the same graph or the flow drifts.
